newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD leader Lafontaine says Kohl must go.
newsitem.headline: German SPD leader Lafontaine says Kohl must go.

text.p: The leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Sunday Chancellor Helmut Kohl was a spent force whose popularity was slumping in voter surveys because he had run out of ideas.
Oskar Lafontaine told national ZDF television the SPD was gaining support because it was working together more effectively than in many years.

"We need a new political start in Germany and I am convinced that the weak opinion polls for the Christian Democrats reflect the fact that people see no chance of a new start with Kohl," Lafontaine said.
"They hold him and his policies responsible for post-war record levels of unemployment and state debt."
A survey released on Sunday by the Emnid institute gave the SPD leading 38 percent of the vote compared to 37 percent for Kohl's party.
The Greens, likely coalition partner for the SPD, had 10 percent while Kohl's coalition partners, the liberal Free Democrats, got four percent -- not enough to re-enter parliament.

Lafontaine appeared to signal he might be prepared to let his SPD arch-rival Gerhard Schroeder challenge Kohl next year for the post of chancellor by saying opinion polls would play a part in the decision.

Schroeder, the popular pro-business state premier of Lower Saxony, consistently beats Kohl in surveys while the left-leaning Lafontaine, who Kohl crushed in the 1990 general election, usually trails the chancellor.
"The decision will not be made by me or Gerhard Schroeder," Lafontaine said. "It will be made by the party leadership..."

"Naturally the opinion polls will play a role as will the candidate's ability to lead the government effectively. And of course the programme will play a role because the government we form should implement the SPD's programme."
Lafontaine said he did not think the high-profile divorce which Schroeder is currently involved in should be exploited by his political opponents.
"I believe that politicians should stick to the agreement not to intervene in private matters and refrain from dragging them into politics," he said.

Lafontaine blamed Kohl for the collapse of tax reform efforts this summer, and said the government should be ashamed of itself for proposals that would have cut taxes on millionaires by 100,000 marks ($54,000) a year.

"We want a reform where the average household will have its tax burden cut by 2,500 marks," he said. "A reform that would allow Helmut Kohl to save 30,000 marks or would save me 25,000 marks is completely irresponsible and will not become law."
The SPD used its control of the upper house of parliament to block Kohl's tax reform programme.
Lafontaine said he regretted that Kohl appeared to be electioneering more than a year before the September 1998 general election.
"He is simply overwhelmed in his office," Lafontaine said. "With unemployment as high as it is, you can't just say okay, now we'll start the election campaign." ($ = 1.846 German Marks)
